summary: ENUM domain names are tied to E.164 telephone numbers, so one must check that the registrant of an ENUM domain is also the assignee of the number. This informational document describes the requirements and a high-level architecture for that validation infrastructure.

plainLanguage.summary: ENUM lets a phone number be looked up as a domain name. Because those names are tied to telephone numbers, the memo sets out who must check that the person registering the name really is the holder of the number, and how that check is repeated over time.

questions: how is an enum domain name revoked
subtitle: How to check that whoever registers an ENUM domain name is the person or company that owns the phone number behind it.

tldr.problem: ENUM domain names are tied to telephone numbers, so unlike ordinary domain names they cannot simply be registered on a first-come-first-served basis by anyone.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a Validation Entity that checks that the applicant is the assignee of the number, and describes the roles around it, the registration and revalidation workflow, and the trust relations each variant needs.
tldr.outcome: The document is an architecture rather than a specification: the validation methods themselves are left to local policy and regulation.

today: RFC 4725 is an Informational memo published in November 2006, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It describes an architecture rather than a protocol: the validation methods themselves are left to local policy and regulation.

sections.title: Why ENUM Needs Validation
sections.content:
E.164 Number Mapping (ENUM) uses the Domain Name System to refer from E.164 numbers, the international telephone numbers, to Uniform Resource Identifiers. The numbers are mapped to domain names by the means described in RFC 3761.

Ordinary domain names are usually allocated on a first-come-first-served basis, and the registration data is the complete source of ownership. ENUM domain names are different, because they are linked to E.164 numbers and so are tied to the status and to the Assignee of the corresponding number.

Preserving the integrity between ENUM and E.164 is one of the main concerns in ENUM implementations, and often one of the reasons why trials precede commercial implementations. Registration processes must make sure of four things over the whole lifetime of a delegation. The ENUM domain name must correspond either to an assigned E.164 number or to one that is assigned during the registration process itself. The number must be within a range approved for use with ENUM. The registration must be authorized by the Assignee, meaning the entity asking for it is either the Assignee or an entity authorized to act for the Assignee. And the Registrant of the ENUM domain must be identical to the Assignee of the number.

Checking these at registration time is commonly called initial validation. On top of that, provisions have to be made for the delegation to be revoked when the requirements are no longer met, so that the state of the ENUM domain name tracks any change in the state and ownership of the number. That regular check is commonly called recurring validation, or revalidation. These requirements are usually part of the local registration policy issued by whoever is in charge of ENUM administration.

sections.title: The Roles In The Provisioning Model
sections.content:
These requirements lead to a new role in the provisioning model, the Validation Entity. The other roles are established ones. A Number Assignment Entity assigns E.164 numbers to end users. Often, but not always, the communication service provider of the end user acts as the Number Assignment Entity. There are two variants of assignment: indirect, where the national number plan administrator gives ranges of numbers to service providers, who then assign numbers or blocks of numbers to their customers and so act as the Number Assignment Entity; and direct, where in certain cases the administrator assigns numbers straight to end users, typically for special purpose numbers such as premium rate.

Because the subscriber data associated with a number is the primary source of assignment information, the Number Assignment Entity usually holds the authoritative information needed to confirm an assignment. A service provider acting as the Number Assignment Entity can therefore easily assert the assignment for its subscribers, and some of them operate databases of subscriber information that authorized entities, such as other providers, can reach in real time under contract for billing and validation. Those databases could be reused for ENUM validation. Number portability complicates this, because the provider that originally acted as the Number Assignment Entity no longer has authoritative information about ported numbers, and whether the old or the new provider acts for them depends on local policy. It is also unlikely that all providers acting as Number Assignment Entities will take part in ENUM validation.

The Assignee is the person or organization to whom the Number Assignment Entity assigns the number, and has the right to use it. The Registrant is the end user who holds the ENUM domain name and usually controls it and its DNS zone content. The Validation Entity verifies whether the Registrant of an ENUM domain name is identical to the Assignee of the corresponding number, and often also whether the entity asking for the registration is the Assignee or is authorized to act for it. That role may be performed by several parties, and the methods used vary with the party, the data sources, the Assignee's choice and the regulatory requirements; the methods themselves are out of scope.

The Registry operates the master database of ENUM domain delegations and runs the authoritative nameservers for the relevant zone under e164.arpa; there must always be a single authoritative ENUM Registry for a given zone. The Registrar performs the delegations on behalf of a Registrant by interacting with the Registry, typically through a protocol like the Extensible Provisioning Protocol, much as registrars do for ordinary domain names. A Registrar may well not be the same entity as the provider of the Registrant, and may therefore lack authoritative assignment information; if it is the same entity, or has a source of authoritative data, it could play the Validation Entity role itself. In any case a Registrar has to ensure proper validation through a Validation Entity before registering a name. The DNS service provider operates the nameservers for the ENUM DNS zones, which hold the NAPTR records, and is usually not involved in validation. The Application service provider operates a service for the Registrant, such as an IP telephony service that populates the ENUM zone so that others can discover the customer's URI, and is also usually not involved in validation. An entity can act in more than one role at once.
sections.plainLanguage: The new role is the Validation Entity, which checks that the applicant really is the holder of the telephone number. Around it sit the registry that keeps the master list, the registrar that does the paperwork, the body that assigns numbers, and the providers that run the servers and the service.

sections.title: The Validation Workflow
sections.content:
The initial validation workflow has five steps. A potential Registrant approaches a Registrar and orders an ENUM domain name. The Registrar chooses a cooperating Validation Entity and requests an initial validation for the name ordered. The Validation Entity performs the actual validation, which could require interaction with the Assignee or Registrant. It reports the result back to the Registrar. And if the validation succeeded, the Registrar provisions the ENUM domain name with the Registry, possibly including validation-related information, depending on the local Registry policy.

In most cases local policy puts an expiry date on a successful validation, and keeping the delegation beyond that date means recurring validation has to be performed. The revalidation workflow has four steps before the possible suspension. The Registrar asks the Validation Entity to revalidate the domain name well before the current validation expires. The Validation Entity checks whether the delegation requirements are still met, possibly using information acquired during the initial validation or associated with the registration data. It reports the result to the Registrar. And if the revalidation succeeded, the delegation may persist, and local Registry policy may require the registration data to be updated, especially if the Registry keeps validation-related expiry information. If the revalidation failed, the delegation must be suspended, either by explicit interaction with the Registry or, if the Registry holds validation-related information, automatically when the current validation expires. Local policy may grant a grace period on the expiry date.

The workflow implies a set of trust relations. The Registry trusts the Validation Entities to enforce the local validation policy, and the Registrars trust the Validation Entities to perform validation properly when asked. What the Registry has to trust depends on how much validation data it receives. If it receives none, it has to trust the Registrar that validation was performed and that the registrar will remove delegations whose revalidation fails. If it receives data including an expiry date but has no way to check that the data is authentic, it has to trust the Registrar for that as well. If it receives data including an expiry date and a way to verify its authenticity, such as a cryptographic signature issued by the Validation Entity, no extra trust relations are needed.

Three regular data flows follow. Registrars and Validation Entities need a standardized protocol and data format, since a registrar may work with several Validation Entities and a Validation Entity may serve several registrars. If local Registry policy says validation information is stored with the delegation records, that information should be embedded in the existing Registry-Registrar flow. And Validation Entities may need to talk to Assignees, but because the form of that communication varies greatly it makes no sense to specify data formats for it.
sections.plainLanguage: The check happens once when the name is registered and then again before it expires. If the second check fails, the name has to be pulled out of the DNS. What the registry has to trust depends on how much proof it is given.

sections.title: Two Example Scenarios
sections.content:
The first scenario assumes the Registrar, the Validation Entity and the Number Assignment Entity are all the same organization, such as an Internet telephony service provider that was assigned number ranges and hands numbers to its customers. The provider assigns an E.164 number together with the matching ENUM domain name and can therefore do the validation simply by looking in its own subscriber database. The provider receives the order, assigns a free number and validates at the same time, sends the ENUM registration to the Registry, possibly with details of the validation applied, and confirms the number assignment and the registration to the customer, who is now both Assignee and Registrant. The memo notes that this is quite close to an ordinary domain name registration.

The second scenario assumes every role is done by a different organization. The ENUM domain name to be registered is based on an already assigned E.164 number, and the Number Assignment Entity gives the Validation Entity access to the subscriber database. There is also a requirement for the Validation Entity to verify the intention of the Assignee, so the process involves contacting the Assignee as well. The Number Assignment Entity assigns the number, which might have happened long before the ENUM registration, for instance when the customer first took a telephony service. The Assignee orders the matching ENUM domain name at a Registrar of their choice. The Registrar asks an independent Validation Entity to validate. The Validation Entity consults the subscriber database of the Number Assignment Entity to check that the Assignee of the number matches the Registrant of the name. When that check is positive, the Validation Entity calls back the number being registered, sets up authentication, and asks the Assignee to confirm the intention, documenting the confirmation. It then returns a positive answer to the Registrar, which may carry the expiry date and the validation method used. Finally the Registrar sends the ENUM registration to the Registry, possibly with more details of the validation.
sections.plainLanguage: Two examples. In the simple one the phone company that owns the number also does the check, so it is much like registering a normal domain name. In the complex one the check is done by an independent body, which looks at the provider's records and then rings the number back to confirm with the customer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A situation where an entity has control over the ENUM domain of a third party's E.164 number carries a high fraud potential. Unauthorized control over the ENUM domain of a bank could, for example, be used for man-in-the-middle attacks on telephone banking applications, and cases of such attacks could discredit ENUM as a whole. Implementing high-quality validation processes is therefore crucial to any ENUM deployment and should receive high attention.

When handling Assignee data, privacy and discretion issues have to be considered. Implementations that transport Assignee data over the Internet must use authenticated and encrypted transport protocols, and the local registration and validation policy and the agreements behind it should clearly limit the use of that data.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk is fraud. If someone can take control of the name behind someone else's number, they can intercept calls, so the validation has to be good. And the subscriber data used to do the check is private, so it must travel encrypted and be used only for that.

items.title: Initial validation
items.text: The Registrar asks a Validation Entity to check the registration before the name is delegated.

items.title: Expiry
items.text: Local policy usually puts an expiry date on a successful validation.

items.title: Revalidation
items.text: Before the expiry, the Registrar asks for the name to be checked again.

items.title: Suspension
items.text: If revalidation fails, the delegation must be suspended, either by the Registrar or automatically when the validation expires.
